title: What happens to unvested RSUs when you get laid off?
summary: Unvested RSUs are usually forfeited when you’re laid off, and vested shares stay yours. What to check, what you can ask for, and how the taxes work.
body_markdown:
## How are RSUs and severance taxed?


**RSUs are wages.** The IRS treats stock-settled RSUs as income in the year the shares are transferred to you, at their fair market value, and they’re reported on your W-2. They’re also subject to Social Security and Medicare taxes. If your severance includes accelerated vesting, the accelerated shares are taxed the same way, in the year they’re delivered.


**Withholding often falls short.** Employers often treat RSU income as supplemental wages, a category IRS Publication 15 says includes bonuses and severance pay, and can withhold federal income tax on it at a flat 22%. Above $1 million of supplemental wages in a year, the rate is 37%. In 2026, the 24% bracket starts at $105,700 of taxable income for single filers ($211,400 married filing jointly), so if you had a strong income year before the layoff, 22% may not cover what you owe. It’s worth estimating your full-year tax now rather than in April.


**Severance pay is taxable income.** IRS Publication 525 says you must include severance in income, and it’s subject to Social Security, Medicare and income tax withholding.


**Your cost basis is the vest-date value.** When you sell, compare the sale price with the value that was taxed at vesting, not with zero. Check that the basis on your Form 1099-B reflects this. If it doesn’t, the Form 8949 instructions explain how to report the correct basis.


**Holding period sets the rate on any gain.** Shares held more than one year after vesting get long-term capital gains rates of 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on your income. Shares held a year or less are taxed at ordinary income rates.


If any of this applies to a large amount, a tax professional can model your year before you sell or sign.
